title: Marina del Rey
name: Marina del Rey
metaTitle: 1031 Exchange Advisory in Marina del Rey, CA
metaDescription: Marina del Rey 1031 exchange advisory for owners of County ground-lease apartments and marina-serving retail, addressing leasehold like-kind rules and thin inventory.

sections.html: Marina del Rey is unusual among Los Angeles submarkets because most of the land underneath its apartment towers, restaurants, and boat slips is not owned outright by the operator sitting on it. Los Angeles County owns the underlying land across most of the harbor and leases parcels to developers on long ground leases, which means a Marina del Rey seller is typically trading a leasehold interest rather than a fee-simple property, and that distinction changes how the exchange has to be structured from the first phone call.

sections.heading: Leasehold Interests and What Counts as Like-Kind Here
sections.html:
Under the regulations, a leasehold with thirty years or more remaining, counting renewal options, is treated as real property comparable to a fee interest for exchange purposes. Marina del Rey ground leases were mostly written with multi-decade terms, but an owner needs to check the remaining term on the actual lease rather than assume every waterfront parcel still clears that threshold, since leases signed decades ago are closer to expiration than a buyer touring the property might guess.

That check matters twice: once to confirm the relinquished property still qualifies, and again on any replacement leasehold under consideration, since a shorter remaining term can quietly disqualify a property that otherwise looks like a clean match.

sections.heading: The Narrow Set of Assets Actually Available Here
sections.html:
Marina del Rey's build-out is essentially fixed, since the harbor and its surrounding parcels have been developed for decades with little room for new construction. What an owner is realistically choosing among includes:

  • Waterfront apartment towers on County ground leases
  • Marina-serving restaurant and retail buildings
  • Boat slip and dry-storage leasehold interests
  • Small office space tied to yacht brokerage and marine services
  • DST interests for owners who want to exit ground-lease management entirely

sections.heading: Financing a Ground-Lease Property
sections.html:
Lenders underwrite leasehold financing differently than a fee-simple loan, and the remaining lease term drives the loan term a bank will offer far more than it would for comparable inland property, since the lender needs the loan to mature well before the lease does. A buyer should get the lender's read on remaining term early, because a Marina del Rey property with twenty-eight years left on its ground lease can still be a fine investment, it just will not finance or exchange the same way as one with fifty years left.

Reassessment under Proposition 13 also applies at transfer, and a buyer should ask their advisor how a leasehold interest is reassessed differently than the fee interest the County retains, since that split affects the going-forward property tax number used in underwriting.

sections.heading: Where a Marina del Rey Exchange Can Stall
sections.html: Because inventory here is so limited, an owner who waits to start the replacement search until after closing on the relinquished property often finds the forty-five day identification window has run out before a qualifying leasehold replacement even surfaces. Coordinating with a qualified intermediary before listing the relinquished property, rather than after, gives an owner more room to confirm lease terms, financing, and identification strategy without racing the clock on a market this thin.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Ground-Lease Purchase Beyond the Sale Price
sections.html:
A numbers-first budget for a Marina del Rey replacement needs to carry ground rent as its own line item, since most leases include a fixed or periodically adjusted rent payable to the County on top of any debt service on the improvements. That ground rent should be modeled against the remaining lease term, not treated as a flat number that holds steady for the life of the investment, since many leases include scheduled step-ups or reappraisal-based resets partway through the term.

Lifecycle cost planning also has to account for the fact that major capital improvements near the end of a ground lease carry more risk, since the improvement's useful life can outlast the lease itself if the remaining term is short. An owner should size any renovation budget against the years left on the lease rather than against a standard building-age depreciation schedule, and should confirm with counsel how the lease treats improvements at expiration before committing capital.

faqs.q: Can a Marina del Rey ground lease actually qualify as like-kind property in an exchange?
faqs.a: A leasehold with thirty years or more remaining, including renewal options, is generally treated as real property comparable to a fee interest. An owner should confirm the remaining term on the specific lease rather than assume every Marina del Rey parcel automatically clears that threshold.

faqs.q: Why is Marina del Rey inventory so limited for a 1031 replacement search?
faqs.a: The harbor and its surrounding parcels have been built out for decades with little room for new construction, so the pool of apartment, retail, and marina-related leasehold interests available at any given time is small. Starting the search before the relinquished property closes helps avoid running short on the forty-five day identification window.

faqs.q: Does financing work the same for a ground-lease property as it does for fee-simple real estate?
faqs.a: No. Lenders size the loan term around the years remaining on the ground lease, since the loan needs to mature well before the lease does. A buyer should get a lender's read on remaining term early rather than assuming a Marina del Rey property will finance the same way as comparable inland real estate.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange Los Angeles confirm my Marina del Rey leasehold qualifies for an exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates planning, property identification, and communication among an investor's advisors. Whether a specific leasehold interest qualifies is a determination made by the investor's CPA, tax attorney, and qualified intermediary.
